source_text: ΤΟΥ ΕΝ ΑΓΙΟΙΣ ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΗΜΩΝ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΙΟΥ Ἀρχιεπισκόπου Καισαρείας Καππαδοκίας ΟΜΙΛΙΑΙ θʹ ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΕΞΑΗΜΕΡΟΝ ΟΜΙΛΙΑ αʹ ̓Εν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν. 1.1 Πρέπουσα ἀρχὴ τῷ περὶ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου συστάσεως μέλλοντι διηγεῖσθαι, ἀρχὴν τῆς τῶν ὁρωμένων διακοσμήσεως προθεῖναι τοῦ λόγου. Οὐρανοῦ γὰρ καὶ γῆς ποίησις παραδί δοσθαι μέλλει, οὐκ αὐτομάτως συνενεχθεῖσα, ὥς τινες ἐφαντάσθησαν, παρὰ δὲ τοῦ Θεοῦ τὴν αἰτίαν λαβοῦσα. Ποία ἀκοὴ τοῦ μεγέθους τῶν λεγομένων ἀξία; πῶς παρεσ κευασμένην ψυχὴν πρὸς τὴν τῶν τηλικούτων ἀκρόασιν προσῆκεν ἀπαντᾶν; Καθαρεύουσαν τῶν παθῶν τῆς σαρκὸς, ἀνεπισκότητον μερίμναις βιωτικαῖς, φιλόπονον, ἐξεταστικὴν, πάντοθεν περισκοποῦσαν εἴ ποθεν λάβοι ἀξίαν ἔννοιαν τοῦ Θεοῦ. Ἀλλὰ πρὶν ἐξετάσαι τὴν ἐν τοῖς ῥήμασιν ἀκρίβειαν, καὶ διερευνήσασθαι ἡλίκα τῶν μικρῶν φωνῶν τούτων ἐστὶ τὰ σημαινόμενα, ἐνθυμηθῶμεν τίς ὁ διαλεγόμενος ἡμῖν. Διότι κἂν τῆς βαθείας καρδίας τοῦ συγγραφέως μὴ ἐφικώ μεθα διὰ τὸ τῆς διανοίας ἡμῶν ἀσθενὲς, ἀλλὰ τῇ γε ἀξιο πιστίᾳ προσέχοντες τοῦ λέγοντος, αὐτομάτως εἰς συγκατά θεσιν τῶν εἰρημένων ἐναχθησόμεθα Μωϋσῆς τοίνυν ἐστὶν ὁ τὴν συγγραφὴν ταύτην καταβαλλόμενος· Μωϋσῆς ἐκεῖνος ὁ μαρτυρηθεὶς ἀστεῖος εἶναι παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ, ἔτι ὑπομάζιος ὤν· ὃν εἰσεποιήσατο μὲν ἡ θυγάτηρ τοῦ Φαραὼ, ἐξέθρεψε δὲ βασιλικῶς, τοὺς σοφοὺς τῶν Αἰγυπτίων διδασκάλους αὐτῷ τῆς παιδεύσεως ἐπιστήσασα. Ὃς τὸν ὄγκον τῆς τυραννίδος μισήσας, καὶ πρὸς τὸ ταπεινὸν τῶν ὁμοφύλων ἀναδραμὼν, εἵλετο συγκακουχεῖσθαι τῷ λαῷ τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἢ πρόσκαιρον ἔχειν ἁμαρτίας ἀπόλαυσιν. Ὁ τὴν πρὸς τὸ δίκαιον φιλίαν ἐξ αὐτῆς τῆς φύσεως κεκτημένος, ὅπου γε καὶ πρὶν ἐπιτραπῆναι αὐτῷ τοῦ λαοῦ τὴν ἀρχὴν, φαίνεται διὰ τὸ τῆς φύσεως μισοπόνηρον μέχρι θανάτου τοὺς κακοὺς ἀμυνόμενος. Ὁ φυγαδευθεὶς παρὰ τῶν εὐεργετηθέντων, καὶ ἀσμένως μὲν τοὺς Αἰγυπτιακοὺς θορύβους ἀπολιπὼν, τὴν δὲ Αἰθιοπίαν καταλαβὼν, κἀκεῖ πᾶσαν σχολὴν ἀπὸ τῶν ἄλλων ἄγων, καὶ ἐν τεσσαράκοντα ὅλοις ἔτεσιν τῇ θεωρίᾳ τῶν ὄντων ἀποσχολάσας. Ὃς ὀγδοηκοστὸν ἤδη γεγονὼς ἔτος, εἶδε Θεὸν ὡς ἀνθρώπῳ ἰδεῖν δυνατὸν, μᾶλλον δὲ ὡς οὐδενὶ τῶν ἄλλων ὑπῆρξε κατὰ τὴν μαρτυρίαν αὐτὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὅτι Ἐὰν γένηται προφήτης ὑμῶν τῷ Κυρίῳ, ἐν ὁράματι αὐτῷ γνωσθήσομαι, καὶ ἐν ὕπνῳ λαλήσω αὐτῷ. Οὐχ οὕτως ὡς ὁ θεράπων μου Μωϋσῆς, ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ οἴκῳ μου πιστός ἐστι· στόμα κατὰ στόμα λαλήσω αὐτῷ, ἐν εἴδει, καὶ οὐ δι' αἰνιγμάτων. Οὗτος τοίνυν ὁ τῆς αὐτοπρο σώπου θέας τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐξίσου τοῖς ἀγγέλοις ἀξιωθεὶς, ἐξ ὧν ἤκουσε παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ διαλέγεται ἡμῖν. Ἀκούσωμεν τοίνυν ἀληθείας ῥημάτων οὐκ ἐν πειθοῖς σοφίας ἀνθρωπίνης, ἀλλ' ἐν διδακτοῖς Πνεύματος λαληθεῖσιν· ὧν τὸ τέλος οὐχ ὁ τῶν ἀκουόντων ἔπαινος, ἀλλ' ἡ σωτηρία τῶν διδασκο μένων. 1.2 Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν. Ἵστησί μου τὸν λόγον τὸ θαῦμα τῆς διανοίας. Τί πρῶτον εἴπω; πόθεν ἄρξομαι τῆς ἐξηγήσεως; Ἐλέγξω τῶν ἔξω τὴν ματαιότητα; ἢ ἀνυμνήσω τὴν ἡμετέραν ἀλήθειαν; Πολλὰ περὶ φύσεως ἐπραγματεύσαντο οἱ τῶν Ἑλλήνων σοφοὶ, καὶ οὐδὲ εἷς παρ' αὐτοῖς λόγος ἕστηκεν ἀκίνητος καὶ ἀσάλευτος, ἀεὶ τοῦ δευτέρου τὸν πρὸ αὐτοῦ καταβάλ λοντος· ὥστε ἡμῖν μηδὲν ἔργον εἶναι τὰ ἐκείνων ἐλέγχειν· ἀρκοῦσι γὰρ ἀλλήλοις πρὸς τὴν οἰκείαν ἀνατροπήν.
thought_title: Moses as trustworthy witness to creation
orientation: Basil opens his first homily on the Six Days by introducing Moses as the divinely attested author whose account of creation demands a prepared and attentive soul.
pass_a_gloss: A fitting beginning for the one about to narrate the constitution of the world is to set before the discourse the beginning of the ordering of visible things. For the making of heaven and earth is about to be handed down, not brought together spontaneously, as some imagined, but having received its cause from God. What hearing is worthy of the greatness of the things said? How ought a prepared soul to come to the hearing of such great things? One cleansed of the passions of the flesh, unshadowed by life's cares, industrious, inquiring, looking around from every side to see if from anywhere it might receive a worthy thought of God. But before examining the precision in the words, and searching out how great are the meanings of these small utterances, let us consider who is the one conversing with us. Because even if we do not reach the deep heart of the writer because of the weakness of our understanding, yet attending to the trustworthiness of the speaker, we shall be led of our own accord to assent to what has been said. Moses then is the one laying down this writing; Moses, that one who was testified to be pleasing to God while still an infant; whom the daughter of Pharaoh adopted, and raised royally, setting the wise teachers of the Egyptians over him for his education. Who, having hated the bulk of tyranny, and having run back to the lowliness of his kinsmen, chose to suffer hardship with the people of God rather than to have the temporary enjoyment of sin. Who possessed friendship toward righteousness from nature itself, since even before the rule of the people was entrusted to him, he appears, because of his nature's hatred of evil, defending against the wicked even to death. Who was exiled by those he had benefited, and gladly left the Egyptian troubles, and reached Ethiopia, and there spent all his leisure away from other things, and for forty whole years devoted his leisure to the contemplation of realities. Who, having already reached his eightieth year, saw God as it is possible for a human to see, or rather as it was granted to no other, according to the very testimony of God: 'If there arises a prophet of yours to the Lord, in a vision I will be known to him, and in sleep I will speak to him. Not so as my servant Moses; in my whole house he is faithful; mouth to mouth I will speak to him, in visible form, and not through riddles.' This one then, deemed worthy of the face-to-face vision of God equally with the angels, speaks to us from what he heard from God. Let us hear then words of truth spoken not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in teachings of the Spirit; whose end is not the praise of the hearers, but the salvation of those being taught. 'In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth.' The wonder of the thought stops my speech. What shall I say first? From where shall I begin the explanation? Shall I refute the vanity of those outside? Or shall I hymn our truth? Much about nature did the wise men of the Greeks work out, and not one account among them stands unmoved and unshaken, the later one always overthrowing the one before him; so that we have no work in refuting their arguments; for they suffice each other for their own overthrow.

choices.why: Fixed glossary term for the temporal beginning of creation; must not be rendered as 'at the start' or 'in principle'.
Fixed glossary term emphasizing God's deliberate act of creation rather than emanation or chance.
Renders the noun for a written composition; 'account' would blur the emphasis on Moses as author of a written text.
The adjective describes Moses as acceptable or pleasing to God; 'beautiful' would miss the relational sense of divine approval.
Keeps the metaphor of oppressive weight or mass; 'pomp' or 'grandeur' would soften the negative force.
Preserves the passive verbal adjective 'taught' and the genitive of source; 'taught by the Spirit' would shift the construction.
rejected: in words taught by the Spirit

pass_b_english: A fitting beginning for one who is about to speak of the constitution of the world is to set before his discourse the beginning of the ordering of visible things. For the making of heaven and earth is about to be handed down to us—not brought together by chance, as some have imagined, but receiving its cause from God. What hearing is worthy of the greatness of what is said? How ought a soul to come prepared for the hearing of such things? It should be pure from the passions of the flesh, unclouded by worldly cares, diligent, searching, looking around from every side to see if it might gain a worthy thought of God. But before we examine the precision in the words and search out how great are the meanings of these small utterances, let us consider who it is who speaks with us. For even if we cannot reach the deep heart of the writer because of the weakness of our understanding, yet if we attend to the trustworthiness of the speaker, we shall be led of our own accord to assent to what is said. Moses, then, is the one who laid down this writing—that Moses who was testified to be pleasing to God while still an infant; whom the daughter of Pharaoh adopted and raised in royal fashion, appointing the wise men of the Egyptians as teachers for his education. He hated the bulk of tyranny and ran back to the lowliness of his own people, choosing to suffer hardship with the people of God rather than to have the temporary enjoyment of sin (Hebrews 11:25). He possessed friendship with righteousness from nature itself, since even before the rule of the people was entrusted to him, he is seen defending against the wicked even to the point of death because of his natural hatred of evil. He was driven into exile by those he had benefited, and gladly left behind the disturbances of Egypt and came to Ethiopia, and there, keeping himself entirely free from other pursuits, he spent forty whole years in the contemplation of realities. When he was already eighty years old, he saw God as far as it is possible for a human being to see—or rather, as it was granted to no one else, according to the very testimony of God: “If there is a prophet among you, I the Lord will make myself known to him in a vision, and I will speak to him in sleep. Not so with my servant Moses; he is faithful in all my house. Mouth to mouth I will speak to him, in visible form, and not in riddles” (Numbers 12:6-8). This man, then, who was counted worthy of the face-to-face vision of God equally with the angels, speaks to us from what he heard from God. Let us listen, then, to words of truth spoken not in persuasive words of human wisdom but in teachings of the Spirit, whose end is not the praise of the hearers but the salvation of those who are taught.

“In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). The wonder of the thought stops my speech. What shall I say first? Where shall I begin the explanation? Shall I refute the vanity of those outside, or shall I praise our truth? The wise men of the Greeks wrote much about nature, and not one doctrine among them has stood fixed and unshaken, since each one always overthrows the one before him. So there is no need for us to refute their teachings, for they are sufficient for one another's overthrow.

last_rejected.why: The citation of Hebrews 11:25 is wrong; Basil paraphrases Exodus 2, not Hebrews.
last_rejected.fix: Remove the parenthetical citation; Basil is narrating Moses' life, not quoting Hebrews.
last_rejected.ruling: ἁμαρτίας ἀπόλαυσιν directly echoes Hebrews 11:25's wording; citation aids readers, not misleading.

last_rejected.why: The opening scriptural verse and its introduction are entirely omitted from the English.
last_rejected.fix: Add before 1.1: '"In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth" (Genesis 1:1).'
last_rejected.ruling: Genesis 1:1 appears in English: 'In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth' with citation.

last_rejected.why: 'Bulk' suggests physical mass; ὄγκος here means pomp/splendor/ostentation of tyranny.
last_rejected.ruling: ὄγκος can mean bulk/mass/magnitude; 'bulk of tyranny' is within normal range, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.why: ἀστεῖος means 'fine, comely, noble' (Exodus 2:2 LXX 'goodly'), not 'pleasing to God' which is a different concept.
last_rejected.ruling: ἀστεῖος ranges from 'comely' to 'pleasing'; 'pleasing to God' captures the sense adequately.

last_rejected.why: ἐν εἴδει here means 'in plain sight, openly, clearly' (not 'visible form'); contrast with 'in riddles'.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐν εἴδει can mean 'in visible form/appearance'; contrast with riddles supports this rendering adequately.
